stem: During insertion of an indwelling urinary catheter in an acute-care hospital, which setup is consistent with CDC recommendations?

options.A: Clean gloves, nonsterile supplies, and a reusable lubricant container because acute-care catheterization uses clean technique.
options.B: Aseptic technique with sterile equipment, including sterile gloves, drape, sponges, an appropriate antiseptic or sterile solution for periurethral cleaning, and a single-use lubricant packet.
options.C: Sterile gloves alone are sufficient; the catheter may contact clean bed linen during insertion if resistance is encountered.
options.D: Clean technique is acceptable in acute care unless the client has recurrent urinary infection or impaired immunity.

rationale: CDC recommendation II.C states that urinary catheters in acute-care hospitals should be inserted using aseptic technique and sterile equipment. Recommendation II.C.1 specifies sterile gloves, drape, sponges, an appropriate antiseptic or sterile solution for periurethral cleaning, and a single-use packet of lubricant jelly. Clean technique is described as an acceptable alternative for chronic intermittent catheterization in non-acute-care settings, not routine acute-care indwelling-catheter insertion.
educational_objective: Use aseptic technique and the CDC-specified sterile equipment for indwelling urinary-catheter insertion in acute-care hospitals.
source_organization: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC)
source_document_title: Summary of Recommendations — Guideline for Prevention of Catheter-Associated Urinary Tract Infections
source_locator: II. Proper Techniques for Urinary Catheter Insertion → recommendations II.A, II.C, II.C.1, II.C.3, and II.D.
source_claim_supported: CDC requires aseptic technique and sterile equipment for acute-care urinary-catheter insertion and specifies sterile gloves, drape, sponges, appropriate antiseptic or sterile periurethral solution, and a single-use lubricant packet; clean technique is an alternative for chronic intermittent catheterization in non-acute care.

blueprint_locator: Appendix A, printed p. 26, Safety and Infection Prevention and Control → Standard Precautions/Transmission-Based Precautions/Surgical Asepsis: apply infection-prevention principles and evaluate aseptic technique.
blueprint_topic: Safety and Infection Prevention and Control — aseptic urinary-catheter insertion

source_original.stem: During insertion of an indwelling urinary catheter in an acute-care hospital, which setup is consistent with CDC recommendations?

options.A: Clean gloves, tap water for periurethral cleansing, and a reusable lubricant container.
options.B: Aseptic technique with sterile equipment, including sterile gloves, drape, sponges, appropriate solution, and single-use lubricant.
options.C: Sterile gloves with permission for the catheter to touch clean bed linen if resistance occurs.
options.D: Clean technique unless the client has recurrent urinary infection or major immunosuppression.

source_original.rationale: In acute-care hospitals, CDC recommends aseptic urinary-catheter insertion using sterile equipment. The recommended setup includes sterile gloves, drape and sponges, an appropriate antiseptic or sterile solution for periurethral cleaning, and a single-use lubricant packet.
source_original.source_detail: CDC CAUTI Summary of Recommendations — Proper Urinary Catheter Insertion / acute care: aseptic technique and sterile equipment including sterile gloves, drape, sponges, appropriate solution and single-use lubricant. Current CDC CAUTI recommendations at exact URL; currentness rechecked 2026-08-15. NCSBN first-check: Client Needs — Safe and Effective Care Environment — Safety and Infection Prevention and Control; Reporting of Incident/Event and infection/safety activities as applicable. 2026 NCLEX-RN Test Plan; effective 2026-04-01 through 2029-03-31; currentness rechecked 2026-08-15.

correction_summary: Retained the stem and key. Rewrote distractors to remove unsupported claims about tap water, resistance, and special high-risk exceptions, while preserving realistic confusion between acute-care aseptic insertion and non-acute-care clean intermittent catheterization. Replaced the generic blueprint locator with the exact NCSBN infection-prevention section.

audit_findings.currentness: CDC page dated March 25, 2024 remains current and was rechecked 2026-08-16.
audit_findings.exact_locator: II.C and II.C.1 directly support the correct setup; II.D defines the separate non-acute-care clean-technique context.
audit_findings.claim_audit: All final technique claims are explicit CDC recommendations; no unsupported cleaning fluid or risk-group exception remains.

distractor_audit.A: Incorrect because acute-care insertion requires aseptic technique and sterile equipment.
distractor_audit.B: Directly matches II.C/II.C.1 and is uniquely correct.
distractor_audit.C: Incorrect because sterile gloves alone do not satisfy the full aseptic sterile-equipment setup and contact with nonsterile linen breaches asepsis.
distractor_audit.D: Incorrect because the acute-care recommendation does not depend on recurrent UTI or immune status.

audit_findings.ambiguity_second_answer: Only B matches the stated acute-care setting.
audit_findings.cueing: All options are insertion-technique setups; B is not identifiable by an unrelated topic or numeric cue.
audit_findings.blueprint: NCSBN printed p. 26 explicitly covers aseptic and sterile technique under Safety and Infection Prevention and Control.
audit_findings.independent_second_pass: Confirmed the unresolved antiseptic-solution comparison in II.C.3 does not affect B because B preserves CDC's broader wording 'appropriate antiseptic or sterile solution'.
